issue.issue_text: Whether the onus of proving all the ingredients of an offence is always upon the prosecution and at no stage does it shift to the accused.

facts: The lower courts (Special Judge and High Court) had taken an approach that the Supreme Court found to be incorrect regarding the burden of proof.

The accused, from the initial stage of the investigation and before a formal complaint (F.I.R.) was issued, had produced documents like a bill and receipt to support his defense that he had legitimately purchased certain apparatus.
The prosecution failed to present this exculpatory evidence (evidence favorable to the accused) to the court.
law: The fundamental principle is that the onus of proving all the ingredients of a criminal offence is always upon the prosecution.
This burden of proof never shifts to the accused at any stage of the trial.
The prosecution's burden does not become any less even if the defense put forward by the accused appears to be not credible or even palpably false.
It is only after the prosecution has successfully discharged its burden of proving the essential elements of the crime that the accused may need to explain or controvert the evidence against them.
When an onus does shift to the accused to establish a plea, the standard of proof required is not the same as that which rests upon the prosecution. The accused's burden is lighter.
If the accused's evidence makes their plea probable, they are entitled to the benefit of reasonable doubt.
application: The Supreme Court found that the lower courts were wrong to place the burden on the accused to prove that he had used the money to purchase the apparatus.
The Court determined that the primary burden was on the prosecution to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt, which included eliminating the probability of the accused's defense.
The Court noted that the accused had provided evidence supporting his plea at the very beginning of the investigation. This action indicated the genuineness of his defense.
By establishing the probability of his plea through this evidence, the accused had met his required standard of proof and was therefore entitled to the benefit of the doubt.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the principle, holding that the onus of proving every ingredient of an offense lies constantly and entirely with the prosecution. This burden never shifts to the accused. The Court clarified that only after the prosecution has first established its case beyond a reasonable doubt does the accused need to offer an explanation. Even then, the standard of proof for the accused is much lower; they only need to demonstrate that their defense is probable to be entitled to the benefit of reasonable doubt.

issue.issue_text: Whether the standard of proof for an accused, when the onus shifts to them to establish a plea, is the same as the standard required for the prosecution.

facts: The accused (appellant) claimed to have used certain funds to purchase a piece of apparatus.
At a very early stage of the investigation, even before a formal complaint (F.I.R.) was issued, the accused produced an original receipt for the purchase and gave a copy to the investigating officer.
The lower courts (Special Judge and High Court) placed the burden on the accused to prove that he had in fact purchased the apparatus with the funds in question.
The lower courts found that the accused had failed to discharge this burden of proof.
law: The onus of proving all the ingredients of an offence is always on the prosecution and never shifts to the accused.
Even if the onus to establish a specific plea shifts to the accused, the standard of proof required of them is not the same as the high standard required of the prosecution.
The prosecution must prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt.
The accused's burden is much lower; they only need to present evidence that 'probabilises the plea'. If the accused's version is made probable, they are entitled to the benefit of a reasonable doubt.
application: The Supreme Court found that the approach of the lower courts was incorrect because they applied the wrong standard of proof to the accused's defense.
The Court noted that the standard of proof for the accused is not the same as that for the prosecution.
The Court determined that the accused, by producing the receipt at the initial stage of the investigation, had presented sufficient evidence to make his plea probable.
Once the probability of the accused's plea was established, the Court held that he should have been given the benefit of the doubt.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition that the standard of proof is the same for the accused and the prosecution. The Court held that while the prosecution must prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt, an accused person, when the onus shifts to them, only needs to establish the probability of their plea. If they succeed in doing so, they are entitled to the benefit of the doubt.

issue.issue_text: Whether the lower courts were correct in holding that the burden of proof was on the appellant to prove that he had utilized the money for purchasing the apparatus.

facts: The appellant, a professor, received a draft from the Indian Council of Medical Research (I.C.M.R.) to purchase a specific piece of scientific apparatus.
The prosecution alleged that the appellant misappropriated this money by not buying the new apparatus and instead pretending an older, existing apparatus was the new one.
The appellant's defense was that he did, in fact, use the money to purchase a new apparatus from a different supplier after the original one fell through.
At the very beginning of the investigation, the appellant produced a receipt and other documents to support his claim of having purchased the new apparatus.
law: The standard of proof required for the prosecution in a criminal case is to prove the accused's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
The standard of proof for an accused person presenting a defense is not the same as the prosecution's. The accused only needs to establish the 'probability' of their plea.
Once the accused establishes the probability of their defense, they must be given the benefit of the doubt, unless the prosecution can eliminate that probability.
application: The Supreme Court found that the lower courts (the Special Judge and the High Court) had incorrectly placed the burden of proof squarely on the appellant to prove he had purchased the new apparatus.
The Court noted that the appellant had produced a receipt and other evidence at the very initial stage of the investigation, which established the probability of his defense.

The Court reasoned that once the appellant's plea was shown to be probable, the burden was on the prosecution to demonstrate that the appellant did *not* purchase the apparatus and that his documents were fake. The prosecution failed to do this.

The Court held that the lower courts focused too much on whether the appellant had definitively proven his purchase, instead of considering whether he had raised a probable defense that created reasonable doubt about the prosecution's case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the lower courts' holding. It concluded that the lower courts were wrong to place the burden of proof on the appellant. The Court ruled that the appellant had successfully established the probability of his defense, and since the prosecution failed to disprove it, the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the doubt.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the onus of proving all the ingredients of an offence is always upon the prosecution and at no stage does it shift to the accused.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's case relies on the principle that the ultimate burden of proof remains with the prosecution. While the appellant offered an explanation and evidence for the use of the funds, the fundamental onus to prove criminal misappropriation beyond a reasonable doubt never shifted from the prosecution.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued, in line with the lower courts, that once the appellant admitted to receiving the money back from Messrs Goverdhandas, the burden of fact shifted to him to prove that the amount was utilized for purchasing the apparatus as he claimed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the standard of proof for an accused, when the onus shifts to them to establish a plea, is the same as the standard required for the prosecution.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the standard of proof required for his plea was not proof beyond a reasonable doubt, but a lower standard. He contended that if the evidence presented on his behalf 'probabilises the plea he will be entitled to the benefit'.
respondent_arguments: The respondent, defending the conviction, implicitly argued that the appellant's evidence was insufficient to meet the required standard of proof, as his witnesses were not credible and his explanation was not substantiated.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the lower courts were correct in holding that the burden of proof was on the appellant to prove that he had utilized the money for purchasing the apparatus.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the lower courts were wrong in their finding. He contended that based on the facts and circumstances, he had successfully established his plea and discharged the burden of proof that lay upon him through his defence witnesses, whose testimony substantiated his claim.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the lower courts were correct. They supported the lower courts' disbelief of the appellant's witnesses (characterizing one as a 'purely chance witness') and maintained that the appellant had failed to provide sufficient proof to discharge the burden on him.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The onus of proving all the ingredients of an offence is always upon the prosecution and at no stage does it shift to the accused. This burden does not lessen even if the accused's defence appears incredible or false. Only after the prosecution has discharged this burden does it fall to the accused to explain or controvert the evidence. If an onus does shift to the accused to establish a plea, the standard of proof is lower than that of the prosecution; the accused is entitled to the benefit of reasonable doubt if their evidence probabilises their plea.
obiter: It is no part of the prosecution duty to somehow hook the crook.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that the lower courts had incorrectly shifted the burden of proof to the appellant. The fundamental legal principle is that the onus of proving all ingredients of an offence always rests upon the prosecution and never shifts. Even in cases where an accused must establish a plea, the standard of proof required of them is not the same as that of the prosecution. The accused merely needs to present evidence that makes their plea probable ('probabilises the plea'), and if they succeed in doing so, they are entitled to the benefit of reasonable doubt. In this case, the appellant had met this lower standard, and the lower courts were wrong to hold that he had failed to discharge the burden upon him.
legal_tests_applied: The onus of proving all the ingredients of an offence is always upon the prosecution and at no stage does it shift to the accused.
Even if the onus shifts upon the accused and the accused has to establish his plea, the standard of proof is not the same as that which rests upon the prosecution.
Where the onus shifts to the accused, and the evidence on his behalf probabilises the plea he will be entitled to the benefit of reasonable doubt.
policy_considerations: It is no part of the prosecution duty to somehow hook the crook.
Even in cases where the defence of the accused does not appear to be credible or is palpably false that burden [on the prosecution] does not become any the less.
